title: Daube de Boeuf Provençale
subtitle: Provençal slow-braised beef with olives, orange and herbes de Provence
excerpt: Daube de boeuf is Provence's answer to boeuf bourguignon: beef braised in red wine with olives, orange peel, herbs, and anchovies. Where bourguignon is earthy and rich, the daube is aromatic and fragrant. The orange peel and olives give it a character that is completely Provençal and unlike any other French beef stew.
sourceNotes: Daube is the great beef braise of Provence. The name comes from the daubière, the tall, narrow earthenware pot in which it is traditionally cooked. The anchovy, orange peel, and black olives are the three ingredients that distinguish it from other French beef braises. The anchovies dissolve completely into the sauce and add depth rather than fishiness.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made the day before. The flavour deepens significantly overnight.

content.text: The beef should marinate overnight in the wine. This is optional but improves the depth of the sauce considerably. The anchovies go in whole with the beef and dissolve completely during the long cook -- they add a savoury depth to the sauce that is unlike anything else. The orange peel should be from an unwaxed orange; just use a peeler to cut 3 or 4 strips.

items.prepNote: unwaxed, 4 strips of peel removed with a peeler

content.text: Preheat the oven to 150C. Season {{beef-chuck}} beef with {{salt-table}} salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a large ovenproof pot over high heat. Brown the beef in batches until deep brown on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.

Reduce heat to medium. Add {{onion}} onion and {{carrots}} carrots. Cook for 8 minutes. Add {{garlic}} garlic and {{anchovy-fillets}} anchovies. Cook for 2 minutes, mashing the anchovies into the oil.

Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} tomatoes, {{red-wine}} wine, {{beef-stock}} stock, {{orange}} orange peel, {{thyme-fresh}} thyme, {{rosemary}} rosemary, and {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves. Return the beef. Bring to a simmer. Cover and cook in the oven for 3 to 3.5 hours until the beef is completely tender and the sauce is rich and thick.
Add {{olives-black}} olives for the last 20 minutes. Remove the herb sprigs, bay leaves, and orange peel before serving. Taste for {{salt-table}} salt. Serve with mash, pasta, or crusty bread.

items.symptom: The sauce tastes very wine-forward and sharp
items.cause: The daube needs more time for the wine to mellow.
items.fix: Continue cooking for another 30 to 45 minutes. If still sharp, add a pinch of sugar. The daube is always better the next day -- the wine becomes smooth and integrated overnight.

content.text: The daube is one of the oldest dishes of Provence. It appears in 18th century Provençal cookbooks and was a staple of the region's farmhouse cooking -- a pot left on a low fire all day while the household worked. The daubière is a tall clay pot with a concave lid that was filled with water to keep the top cool and prevent evaporation. The dish is now made in any heavy lidded pot.
